snippet.title: 3 Claude Cowork Features That Will Change How You Use It
snippet.description:
If you've been using Claude Cowork, these are the three features that will completely change how you use it:

First - Skills. This is the one that makes Cowork feel like it was built specifically for you. Skills are essentially custom commands you can trigger to get Claude to do very specific things the way you want them done. Once you set these up they become muscle memory. You stop typing long prompts and start just telling it what you need in one word.

Second - Connectors. You can connect it to the tools you're already using - Gmail, Google Drive, Slack, Notion, Google Calendar, and Claude can actually read and work across all of them at the same time. So when you ask it to prep you for a meeting, it's not just working with what you tell it in the chat. It's pulling from your actual emails, your actual calendar, your actual documents. The context it has access to completely changes the quality of what it can do for you.

Third - Scheduled Tasks. You can tell Cowork to do something at a specific time - run a daily digest every morning, pull a report every Friday, follow up on something next week. You set it once, and it runs without you having to think about it again. This is the closest thing to having an assistant that works while you sleep.

The combination of all three is what makes Cowork feel different from just chatting with AI. It's less of a tool you use and more of a system that works around you.

Which one are you trying first? Drop it in the comments 👇

snippet.title: Browsers Are Dead. Claude Just Replaced Them.
snippet.description:
AI browsers were supposed to be the future. But I think something bigger is happening: Codex and Claude Code are turning into the main place knowledge work gets done.

What i've been working on: https://chorus.com/agents/88be7a2a-c5fc-4fb8-8db3-70598a16aeab

Lenny’s Podcast: https://youtube.com/@LennysPodcast?si=yBPlcuJ5oANQqr0X

Dan Shipper on X: https://x.com/danshipper?s=21


In this video, I break down Dan Shipper’s argument from Lenny’s Podcast, why tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cowork, and Proof matter, and how we’re moving from browser tabs to task tabs.

The big shift is that your AI agent won’t just sit inside an app. Your apps will increasingly be built so your agent can use them with you. That means agent-native document editors, in-app browsers, generative mini apps, and workflows where Codex or Claude can control the browser, read your context, use your tools, and help complete the task directly.

I also share my predictions for where this is going next:

Multiple browser tabs per agent thread
Agents automatically opening the right apps for each task
Agent-native SaaS replacing AI buttons inside traditional software
Generative mini apps that connect to your Gmail, Notion, Docs, Typefully, and other tools
Why you should start organizing your work at the task and SOP level
What I’ve been working on:
My team and I are building an iMessage-first AI agent that runs 24/7, connects to your tools, supports automations, and lets you use models like Claude and Codex from your phone or computer. More about me: rileybrown.xyz

snippet.title: "Just Ask Codex": Inside OpenAI's Own Working Culture | Romain Huet, OpenAI
snippet.description:
What happens when the best engineers at OpenAI stop writing code by hand? How does a coding tool turn into a command center for agents that work for days without you in the loop? And why has Germany quietly become one of OpenAI's top five markets for Codex?
In this episode of AI to the DNA, the podcast for everyone who wants to really understand and apply AI, I sit down with Romain Huet, Head of Developer Experience at OpenAI and one of the key people behind Codex. We meet in Paris at OpenAI's local office, right after the team shipped GPT 5.5 and a wave of new Codex capabilities. Romain previously led product at Stripe and is now building the layer where developers, and increasingly everyone else, meet the models.

Höre den Podcast auch auf deiner Lieblings Podcast Plattform: https://attd.fm/play

We talk about why Codex started as a coding tool, why it became something much bigger, and how OpenAI's own teams, from engineering to finance, now use it as their daily working surface. Romain explains why the jump from GPT 5.2 to 5.3 Codex was the real turning point, and what it means that even the best engineers no longer write code by hand.

From there we go deep into the architecture behind it: the open-source Codex harness, the layer that connects models, tools, files and your computer. We discuss what a harness actually is, why OpenAI made it public, and why prompt engineering as we knew it is essentially gone. We also dig into the harder questions, sandboxing, computer use, prompt injection, and how the new code review capabilities of GPT 5.5 are already preventing real production incidents at companies like Datadog.

Finally, Romain walks us through what excites him most right now: /goal, the command that lets Codex relentlessly pursue an ambitious goal across days of uninterrupted work. We close on a simple but uncomfortable insight: the models are so good now that the real bottleneck has become our own imagination.

I'm Christoph Magnussen and at AI to the DNA, I'm not just asking how to use AI. I’m asking why it works the way it does. This podcast is for everyone who wants to move beyond tool-tourism and master the real craft of AI: Learning to think, work, and build side by side with intelligent systems!
